question.text: Cherry-picking in fund reporting refers to:

answer.text: Selecting the best investments for the portfolio
Selectively presenting only successful investments while hiding poor performers
Picking the best investment team members

explanation.text: The Logic: In fund reporting, "cherry-picking" refers to the practice of selectively highlighting only successful investments — winners — in periodic communications while quietly downplaying or omitting underperforming positions. The result is a distorted view of overall portfolio performance that overstates skill and conceals losses. The Trap: Cherry-picking is not the legitimate exercise of selecting the best investments for the portfolio, not the choice of team members, and not investor selection during fundraising — it is a reporting-disclosure abuse, not a portfolio-construction or hiring activity. Note: The Series XIX-A AIF (Category I and II) Distributors workbook pages reviewed cover periodic disclosures, statutory obligations, confidentiality, and portfolio/deal reporting, but do not explicitly define cherry-picking with the "selectively presenting successful investments while hiding poor performers" framing. The framing above reflects general investment-reporting practice rather than a workbook citation.
